## Introduction

```{r echo=FALSE}
library(revealEquations)
```

$\newcommand{\E}{\mathbb{E}}

\newcommand{\cov}{\mathrm{cov}}

\newcommand{\Corr}{\mathrm{corr}}
\newcommand{\corr}{\mathrm{corr}}
\newcommand{\L}{\mathrm{L}}
\renewcommand{\P}{\mathrm{P}}
\newcommand{\independent}{{\perp\!\!\!\perp}}
\newcommand{\indicator}[1]{ \mathbf{1}\{#1\} }
\newcommand{\ATT}{\text{ATT}}
\newcommand{\ACR}{\text{ACR}}$

[Shift-share]{.alert} (or [Bartik]{.alert}) instruments are everywhere in applied work

* Combine [shares]{.alert-blue} --- how exposed each unit is to each sector --- with [shifts]{.alert-blue} --- aggregate, sector-level shocks

* About one-eighth of all instruments in NBER working papers are explicitly described as shift-share [@borusyak-hull-jaravel-2025]

<br>

[This session:]{.alert} shift-share designs are much [closer to the DiD material from Session 1]{.alert-blue} than they might first appear

* In fact, one of the two main paths to identification is *literally* a DiD design with a continuous treatment

## Why this belongs in this course

Recall the "what's not included" slide from Session 1:

* We ruled out [fuzzy DiD]{.alert} --- binary treatment, aggregate data, policy changes used as an instrument

* We ruled out [heterogeneous adoption designs]{.alert}

<br>

. . .

Shift-share designs sit close to both

* And the [interpretation problems]{.alert} we spent Session 1 on --- weights, selection bias across doses, strong parallel trends --- [do not go away]{.alert-blue} when you call the design an instrument instead of a treatment

## Plan for this Session

<br> <br>

1. Setup, notation, and a running example

2. Two paths to identification: shares vs. shifts

3. The exogenous-shares path *is* DiD with a continuous treatment

4. Rotemberg weights: which comparisons are actually driving the estimate?

5. Inference

6. Practical recommendations

# 1. Setup, notation, and a running example {visibility="uncounted"}

## Notation

- [Units:]{.alert} $i = 1, \ldots, n$ (e.g., counties, commuting zones)

- [Sectors:]{.alert} $j = 1, \ldots, J$ (e.g., industries)

- [Shares:]{.alert} $z_{ij}$ --- unit $i$'s exposure to sector $j$, usually [predetermined]{.alert-blue}, with $\sum_j z_{ij} = 1$

- [Shifts:]{.alert} $g_j$ --- an aggregate shock to sector $j$

. . .

<br>

The [shift-share instrument]{.alert} is
$$B_i = \sum_{j=1}^J z_{ij} \, g_j$$

. . .

used to instrument for an endogenous treatment $X_i$ in
$$Y_i = \beta_0 X_i + \varepsilon_i$$

## Where You Have Seen This Before

| Application | Shares $z_{ij}$ | Shifts $g_j$ |
|---|---|---|
| @bartik-1991, @blanchard-katz-1992 | Local industry employment | National industry growth |
| @card-2001 | Immigrant enclaves by origin | National inflows by origin |
| @autor-dorn-hanson-2013 | Local industry employment | Chinese import growth |
| @downes-2024 | 1910 local industry shares | National unionization by industry |

. . .

<br>

The structure is [always the same]{.alert}: a common set of shocks, and units that differ in [how exposed]{.alert-blue} they are to each one

## The Same Design, Different Labels

Two things worth noticing about that table:

* [The shares are almost always predetermined]{.alert} --- employment shares in a base year, enclaves before the inflow, industry composition decades earlier

* [The shifts are almost always few and aggregate]{.alert} --- one policy, one trade shock, a handful of sectors doing most of the work

. . .

<br>

<mark>Which is to say: most of these are exposure designs, whether or not the authors describe them that way</mark>

* @jaeger-ruist-stuhler-2018 make a related point in the immigration setting --- if past and current inflows are correlated, the enclave instrument confounds short-run and long-run responses

## Running Example: @downes-2024

[Question:]{.alert} Did the expansion of labor unions contribute to the American Baby Boom?

[Setting:]{.alert} The 1935 National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) --- the largest expansion of unionism in U.S. history

* [Treatment $X_{it}$:]{.alert-blue} county-level union membership rate

* [Outcome $Y_{it}$:]{.alert-blue} county-level birth rates (also completed fertility)

. . .

[Endogeneity concern:]{.alert} tight labor markets raise unionization *and* may raise fertility directly

## Running Example: The Instrument

@downes-2024 constructs

$$SSIV_{it} = \sum_{j=1}^J \underbrace{\textrm{NatlUnionRate}_{jt}}_{\textrm{shift}} \times \underbrace{\textrm{IndShare}^{1910}_{ij}}_{\textrm{share}}$$

. . .

* [Shifts:]{.alert-blue} national, industry-level union membership rates over time

* [Shares:]{.alert-blue} local industry composition, measured in [1910]{.alert} --- decades before the NLRA

. . .

[Relevance:]{.alert} some industries were far more amenable to unionization than others (long-lived capital, scarce skilled labor, spatial isolation)

## Running Example: The Comparison Being Made

@downes-2024 gives a concrete two-county example:

* [Cameron County, PA]{.alert-blue} and [Forest County, PA]{.alert-blue} --- similar 1930 population ($\approx 5{,}200$), neither unionized before the NLRA

* But Cameron had more transportation, more coal mining, and more of the manufacturing subindustries that later unionized heavily

. . .

<br>

[The instrument predicts Cameron should unionize more.]{.alert} It did: by 1960, union membership was 26.3% in Cameron vs. 7.7% in Forest

. . .

<mark>Note what this comparison looks like: two units, differing in *how much* they were exposed to a common shock</mark>

# 2. Two paths to identification {visibility="uncounted"}

## Where does the identifying variation come from?

The instrument is built from two ingredients, so there are two ways to argue it is valid

. . .

[Path 1 --- Exogenous shares]{.alert} &nbsp; [@goldsmith-sorkin-swift-2020]

* Few shocks, but lots of variation in exposure to them

* Identification comes from the [shares]{.alert-blue} being as-good-as-randomly assigned (conditional on controls)

. . .

[Path 2 --- Exogenous shifts]{.alert} &nbsp; [@borusyak-hull-jaravel-2022; @adao-kolesar-morales-2019]

* Many shocks, treated as quasi-randomly assigned

* Shares are allowed to be [endogenous]{.alert-blue}

## Which path are you on?

This is a [substantive]{.alert} choice, not a technical one --- and it determines which assumptions you defend, which diagnostics you run, and how you do inference

. . .

@goldsmith-sorkin-swift-2020 suggest you are likely on the [shares]{.alert} path if you:

1. Describe your design as [differential exogenous exposure to common shocks]{.alert-blue}

2. Motivate it with a [two-unit example]{.alert-blue}

3. Emphasize shocks to [specific]{.alert-blue} sectors as central

. . .

<br>

<mark>@downes-2024 does all three --- and says so explicitly: identification "follows from the exogeneity of the shares, rather than the shifts"</mark>

## Why the shares path, here?

Two features of the setting push toward shares:

* [One big shock, not many:]{.alert} the NLRA is essentially a single national event. The "many shocks" asymptotics behind the shifts path are not a good description

* [Shares are genuinely predetermined:]{.alert} 1910 industry composition, 25 years before the policy

. . .

<br>

[This is the case that connects to Session 1]{.alert-blue} --- so it is where we will spend most of our time

* We will come back to the shifts path briefly at the end

# 3. Exogenous shares *is* DiD with a continuous treatment {visibility="uncounted"}

## The Numerical Equivalence Result

@goldsmith-sorkin-swift-2020 show:

::: {.callout-note}
## Equivalence

TSLS using the Bartik instrument $B_i = \sum_j z_{ij} g_j$ is [numerically equivalent]{.alert} to GMM using the [shares $z_{i1}, \ldots, z_{iJ}$ as instruments]{.alert}, with a weight matrix built from the shifts $g_j$
:::

. . .

<br>

[Implication:]{.alert} the exogeneity condition should be stated in terms of the [shares]{.alert-blue}, not the shifts

* The shifts are doing the work of *combining* many instruments, not of *justifying* them

## From shares-as-instruments to DiD

Once the shares are the instruments, the design is an [exposure design]{.alert}: shares measure differential exposure to a common shock

. . .

> "In settings where the researcher has a pre-period, this empirical strategy is just difference-in-differences."
>
> --- @goldsmith-sorkin-swift-2020

. . .

And @borusyak-hull-jaravel-2025 describe the same path as

> "pooling together multiple difference-in-differences designs leveraging heterogeneous shock exposure."

## What is the treatment?

Line up the two setups:

| DiD with continuous treatment | Shift-share (shares path) |
|---|---|
| Dose $D_i$ | Exposure share $z_{ij}$ |
| Common timing of treatment | Common shock $g_j$ |
| $\ATT(d\vert d)$, $\ACR(d)$ | Effect of differential exposure |
| Untreated units: $D_i = 0$ | Units with $z_{ij} \approx 0$ |

. . .

<br>

<mark>The share *is* a continuous treatment. Everything from Session 1 applies.</mark>

## So what carries over from Session 1?

[Good news:]{.alert} the identification logic is familiar

* Compare changes across units with different exposure

* Pre-periods let you assess parallel trends

. . .

[Less good news:]{.alert} all three Session 1 problems come along

1. [Weak parallel trends]{.alert-blue} identifies $\ATT(d|d)$, but *not* causal responses to dose

2. Comparing across doses adds [selection bias]{.alert-blue} terms

3. [Strong parallel trends]{.alert-blue} is needed to interpret dose comparisons causally --- and it is a strong assumption

## Session 1, restated for this setting

Recall the decomposition from Session 1:

$$\underbrace{\ATT(d_h|d_h) - \ATT(d_l|d_l)}_{\textrm{what a dose comparison gives you}} = \underbrace{\E[Y_{t=2}(d_h) - Y_{t=2}(d_l)|D=d_h]}_{\textrm{Causal Response}} + \underbrace{\ATT(d_l|d_h) - \ATT(d_l|d_l)}_{\textrm{Selection Bias}}$$

. . .

In a shift-share design, "comparing across doses" is [exactly what the estimator does]{.alert}

* High-exposure counties vs. low-exposure counties

* The selection bias term asks: would *high*-exposure counties have responded differently to a *low* dose than low-exposure counties did?

. . .

<mark>Nothing about writing this as an IV makes that term disappear</mark>

## @downes-2024 is careful about this

The paper says so directly:

> "In this setup with continuous treatment and the presumption of heterogeneous treatment effects, the ATE is not identified under the classic ('weak') parallel trends assumption [@callaway-goodman-santanna-2026]. The target parameter is therefore an ATT and I interpret any extrapolations of treatment effects across the support of the treatment dose distribution with caution."

. . .

<br>

[This is the right posture]{.alert-blue} --- and it is unusual. Most shift-share papers do not flag it

# 4. Rotemberg weights {visibility="uncounted"}

## Which comparisons drive the estimate?

@goldsmith-sorkin-swift-2020 build on Rotemberg (1983): the Bartik estimator is a [weighted sum of just-identified IV estimators]{.alert}, one per sector

$$\hat{\beta}_{Bartik} = \sum_{j=1}^J \hat{\alpha}_j \, \hat{\beta}_j$$

where $\hat{\beta}_j$ uses share $z_{ij}$ alone as an instrument, and the [Rotemberg weights]{.alert-blue} $\hat{\alpha}_j$ sum to one

. . .

<br>

[Why you care:]{.alert} the weights tell you which exposure designs --- which concrete comparisons --- your estimate actually rests on

* And therefore which identifying assumptions are worth testing

## Reading the weights

Three diagnostics @goldsmith-sorkin-swift-2020 recommend:

1. [How concentrated are the weights?]{.alert} If five sectors carry 40% of the weight, your design is really about those five sectors

2. [Do the shifts explain the weights?]{.alert} If not, the shocks are a poor guide to your identifying variation

3. [Are any weights negative?]{.alert} Negative weights threaten a LATE-like interpretation under heterogeneous effects

. . .

<br>

<mark>This should feel familiar --- it is the same "what are the weights on?" question we asked about TWFE in Session 1</mark>

## Rotemberg weights in @downes-2024

@downes-2024 reports all three:

* Shifts explain only [~21%]{.alert} of the variation in the Rotemberg weights $\Rightarrow$ identifying variation is coming from the [shares]{.alert-blue}, consistent with the stated design

* Negative weights are [~3%]{.alert} of the total $\Rightarrow$ a LATT-like interpretation is defensible

* Event studies using top-weighted industries as separate instruments support parallel trends

. . .

<br>

[This is a good template for what to report]{.alert-blue}

# 5. Inference {visibility="uncounted"}

## Standard errors are a real problem here

@adao-kolesar-morales-2019 run a placebo exercise: generate [random]{.alert} sectoral shocks, build the shift-share regressor, regress actual outcomes on it

. . .

<br>

[Result:]{.alert} tests at a 5% nominal level reject the null of no effect in [up to 55%]{.alert} of placebo samples

. . .

<br>

[Why:]{.alert} regression residuals are correlated across units with [similar sector shares]{.alert-blue} --- even if those units are geographically far apart. Clustering by region does not fix this

## What to do about it

@adao-kolesar-morales-2019 derive inference methods valid under arbitrary cross-unit correlation of this kind

* In practice: confidence intervals can be [substantially wider]{.alert}

. . .

<br>

[Practical point for this course:]{.alert} this is a distinct issue from everything else we have discussed

* Sessions 1--2 were about [what parameter you identify]{.alert-blue}

* This is about [how uncertain you are about it]{.alert-blue}

* Both can go wrong independently

# 6. The other path, briefly {visibility="uncounted"}

## Exogenous shifts

@borusyak-hull-jaravel-2022 develop the complementary framework:

* Identification from [quasi-random assignment of the shocks]{.alert}

* Shares are allowed to be [endogenous]{.alert-blue}

* Rests on an equivalence result of its own: SSIV coefficients can be recovered from a [shock-level]{.alert-blue} regression, so the conditions to check are shock-level conditions

. . .

<br>

[When is this the right frame?]{.alert} Many shocks, plausibly as-good-as-random, and no credible story for why exposure shares are exogenous

## Why we are not emphasizing it here

Two reasons:

1. [It is a different design.]{.alert} The asymptotics run over shocks, not units. The DiD analogy does not carry over cleanly

2. [Our running example is not in it.]{.alert} @downes-2024 has essentially one shock (the NLRA) and strong grounds for predetermined shares

. . .

<br>

<mark>But: the choice between paths should be made on the economics of your setting, not on which one is more convenient</mark>

* @borusyak-hull-jaravel-2025 provide checklists for both

# 7. Practical recommendations {visibility="uncounted"}

## Recommendations

1. [Say which path you are on]{.alert} --- shares or shifts --- and defend *that* assumption

2. If shares: [treat it as a DiD design]{.alert-blue}. Show pre-trends. Show correlates of the shares. Describe the concrete two-unit comparison

3. [Report Rotemberg weights.]{.alert-blue} Concentration, correlation with shifts, negative weights

4. [Be careful interpreting dose comparisons.]{.alert-blue} Weak parallel trends does not license them

    * @chaisemartin-lei-2023 propose alternative estimators for panel IV designs of this type that are robust to heterogeneous effects

5. [Use appropriate standard errors]{.alert-blue} [@adao-kolesar-morales-2019]

## Conclusion

* Shift-share designs are not a separate methodological island --- the [exogenous-shares path is a continuous-treatment DiD design]{.alert}

* That means the Session 1 lessons transfer directly: [weights matter]{.alert-blue}, and [comparing across doses requires more than parallel trends]{.alert-blue}

* The literature has good diagnostic tools (Rotemberg weights, pre-trend tests, valid standard errors) --- they are just not used often enough

. . .

<br>

<mark>If you take one thing away: decide whether your identification comes from shares or shifts, say it out loud, and then defend the assumption you actually need</mark>
